title: Judicial Renaissance -- Ch. 2: The APJR: An Executive Summary
keywords: International Conference and Showcase on Judicial Reforms
primary_topics: Chapter 2 of 'Judicial Renaissance' -- a talk to a Rotary audience giving an executive summary of the Supreme Court's Action Program for Judicial Reform, compressed from over a hundred projects into three headings: the transformation of judges, the judicial work environment, and the judiciary's relationship with its various publics

The case that the APJR has modernized the Philippine judiciary through concrete measures -- bar and legal education reform, Philja training, the New Code of Judicial Conduct, computerization, the e-library, mobile courts and an open information office

The international standing of the program: endorsements, grants and loans from the UNDP, World Bank, ADB and The Asia Foundation and from seven foreign governments, and the World Bank counsel's judgment that other parts of the world 'have much to learn from the Philippine judicial reform program'

A preview of the International Conference and Showcase on Judicial Reforms of November 28-30, 2005, and CJP's insistence that the APJR will outlast Chief Justice Davide's retirement because it belongs to the entire judiciary
sub_topics: His gracious opening to Rotary president Jesus F. Tambunting, Program Director Rene Golangco and his friend Mike Varela of the Philippine Chamber of Commerce and Industry, and the story of how Varela would not take no for an answer

The APJR's six components -- Judicial Systems and Procedures, Institutions Development, Human Resource Development, Integrity Infrastructure Development, Access to Justice by the Poor, and Reform Support Systems -- and the separate Program Management Office created to implement them

Transformation of judges begins with law school: using the Court's constitutional power over admission to the practice of law to steer legal education through the bar examinations, with reforms in test content, computerization, perpetual disqualification of repeat failures and tenured examiners

The Legal Education Board to be headed by a retired SC justice to oversee law colleges and reformulate curricula, and the piloted Judicial Apprenticeship Program exposing third- and fourth-year students to court proceedings, legal research and decision writing
MCLE for practising lawyers and strict enforcement of the lawyer's oath, with 463 lawyers fined, warned, censured, admonished, reprimanded, arrested, suspended or disbarred in six years

The Judicial and Bar Council as the constitutional filter limiting the President's choices, chaired by the Chief Justice with the justice secretary, a senator, a congressman, a retired SC justice and representatives of the bar, academe and private sector

Continuing judicial education under PHILJA through classroom seminars and e-learning, and the P600 million grant being negotiated from the Japanese government for the Philja Training Center in Tagaytay

Ethics: the New Code of Judicial Conduct effective June 1, 2004 patterned on the Bangalore Principles drafted under UN aegis, and 660 justices and judges sanctioned from 1999 to 2004 under the earlier Canons and Code

Rewards and protections: the annual Judicial Excellence Awards, Judge-to-Judge Dialogues with The Asia Foundation, Australian scholarships, the doubling of judicial compensation through 25 percent annual increases from November 2003, better retirement benefits, and dismissal of complaints filed within six months of compulsory retirement

The judicial work environment: total computerization built on the USAID-supported Case Flow Management pilot in Pasay City and the CIDA-supported CAMIS in Metro Manila, now being integrated for nationwide implementation

A Computer Literacy Program for 28,000 judicial officials and employees, a computer in every courtroom with a second within six months, and interest-free 36-month laptop installments at P1,000 a month

The e-library launched in November 2004, with a search engine, Internet access nationwide and CDs for courts without connectivity; the Benchbook for Trial Court Judges in digital and paper versions; and new rules on electronic evidence, intellectual property, corporate rehabilitation, intra-corporate controversies and juveniles

Model electronic courts funded by a World Bank loan, the acquisition of the old GSIS Building on Arroceros Street for a Manila Hall of Justice, alternative dispute resolution projects to unclog dockets, the ADB-funded blueprint on independence and accountability, and the Justice-to-Justice Program with ABA-Asia and USAID

Opening the judicial fortress without compromising the confidentiality of collegiate deliberations: the Public Information Office established in early 1999, publishing Benchmark, Court News and Court News Flash in simple non-legalese and maintaining the Court's website with MISO

Chamber-to-Chamber Dialogues launched with The Asia Foundation to answer business-sector criticism that the judiciary interferes in economic life, reinforced by his book 'Leveling the Playing Field,' and the Justice on Wheels mobile court decongesting jails and resolving family problems

The international conference at the Makati Shangrila: three days of plenary and parallel sessions on independence and integrity, access to justice, and reform management, plus a showcase participants can see, touch and operate, with Chief Justices and judicial educators from about 80 countries attending free of registration fees
The intended outcome of the conference -- an Asia-Pacific Judicial Reform Network as the vehicle for sharing lessons and best practices in the region

The Davao City 'Judge-to-Judge' Dialogue of July 15, 2005 where he was asked what would happen to the APJR after Davide's retirement, and his answer that it will continue because it belongs to everyone from the Supreme Court to the lowliest clerk
signature_phrases: a very comprehensive and all-encompassing program that has six distinct components
to tell our various publics the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth
Its job is not to "sanitize" or "angle" stories.

from the Supreme Court to the lowest court, from the SC justices to the lowliest clerk in the farthest ends of our country
let us hold hands, stand united, and help us pursue our reform program

stances.claim: The APJR is a comprehensive and all-encompassing program whose more than a hundred projects are best understood under three headings -- the transformation of judges, the judicial work environment, and the judiciary's relationship with its publics.
stances.rhetorical_move: executive-summary framing: replacing bureaucratic components with a three-part structure a lay audience can hold in mind

stances.claim: The reforms are real and measurable: 463 lawyers and 660 justices and judges disciplined, judicial pay doubled, a computer in every courtroom, an e-library searchable nationwide, and a mobile court already decongesting jails.
stances.rhetorical_move: proof by enumeration, pairing each reform area with dates, figures and named donors

stances.claim: The Court must open up the judicial fortress to maintain public trust, but without compromising the confidentiality of its collegiate deliberations, which is why the PIO tells the truth rather than sanitizing, angling, proselytizing or propagandizing.
stances.rhetorical_move: balancing transparency against deliberative secrecy, then defining the information office by what it refuses to do

stances.claim: The Philippine program has been acclaimed abroad as a model worth following, with the World Bank's chief counsel saying the APJR is fundamentally well-rooted and well informed and that other parts of the world have much to learn from it.
stances.rhetorical_move: external endorsement quoted verbatim and backed by the roster of institutions and governments funding the program

stances.claim: The APJR will continue after Chief Justice Davide's retirement because, although he envisioned and started it and gathered its support, it is not his personal project but one undertaken by everyone in the judiciary.
stances.rhetorical_move: answering a question put to him in public, then converting the answer into an appeal for unity and continuity

notable_anecdotes: CJP explains how he came to be speaking at all: he had begged off because of the Court's schedule and his conference duties, but ran into Mike Varela at a private luncheon hosted by Swedish Ambassador Annika Markovic, and Varela 'could not be dissuaded.'
He notes that the Philippine Chamber of Commerce and Industry thought so highly of Varela that it named him chairperson emeritus for life.

He recounts a question from the floor at a 'Judge-to-Judge' Dialogue in Davao City on July 15, 2005 -- what happens to the APJR after Davide retires? -- and gives his 'simple and forthright' answer that it will continue because it belongs to the whole judiciary.
He describes the conference showcase as something more than a discussion: the reform projects will be exhibited for participants 'to see, touch, behold, and -- in some cases -- actually operate.'

He points out the scale of donor support behind the gathering: Chief Justices and top magistrates of about 80 countries invited free of registration fees, with complimentary hotel, meals and local travel, and travel grants for developing countries.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 2 of 'Judicial Renaissance' is a talk Justice Panganiban gave to a Rotary audience, offering what he calls an executive summary of the Supreme Court's Action Program for Judicial Reform. After thanking his hosts and explaining that his friend Mike Varela would not accept his refusal, he describes the APJR as a comprehensive program with six components -- Judicial Systems and Procedures, Institutions Development, Human Resource Development, Integrity Infrastructure Development, Access to Justice by the Poor, and Reform Support Systems -- so numerous in its projects that the Court created a separate Program Management Office. Having no time for over a hundred projects, he reorganizes them under three headings. The transformation of judges begins in law school, with the Court using its constitutional power over admission to the practice of law to steer the bar examinations, the coming Legal Education Board, a piloted Judicial Apprenticeship Program, strengthened MCLE and strict enforcement of the lawyer's oath that has seen 463 lawyers sanctioned in six years; it continues with the Judicial and Bar Council as a filter against partisan appointments, PHILJA's classroom and e-learning programs and the P600 million Japanese grant for a training center in Tagaytay, the New Code of Judicial Conduct patterned on the Bangalore Principles, 660 justices and judges disciplined from 1999 to 2004, the Judicial Excellence Awards, Judge-to-Judge Dialogues, Australian scholarships and a doubling of judicial compensation. The second heading covers tools: the USAID-backed Case Flow Management pilot and the CIDA-backed CAMIS, a computer literacy program for 28,000 personnel, computers in every courtroom and installment laptops, the e-library and Benchbook, new rules of procedure, model electronic courts financed by a World Bank loan, the old GSIS building converted into a Hall of Justice, and alternative dispute resolution. The third covers publics: a Public Information Office that exists to tell 'the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth' rather than to sanitize or propagandize, Chamber-to-Chamber Dialogues answering business criticism, and Justice on Wheels. He cites the World Bank's Anthony Gerald Toft that the APJR is 'fundamentally well-rooted' and that others have much to learn from it, previews the November 28-30, 2005 conference and showcase at the Makati Shangrila with its planned Asia-Pacific Judicial Reform Network, and closes with the answer he gave in Davao City: the program will continue after Davide's retirement because it is not his personal project but the work of the entire judiciary.
